paper_title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Practitioners often adapt an instruction-tuned language model to domain by fine-tuning it on questionanswer pairs that state new facts. The facts are learned, but at cost elsewhere. Finetuned on recent biomedical articles, SmolLM3-3B answers 21 points more of the new questions correctly, yet its instruction-following accuracy on IFEval falls from 71% to 9%. Fine-tuning is known to be an ineﬀicient way of adding knowledge (Gekhman et al., 2024; Ovadia et al., 2024). We study how to preserve general assistant behavior during closed-book factual fine-tuning. Where does the damage occur? Standard finetuning sharply lowers accuracy on every benchCorresponding author: xfshi@baai.ac.cn. 1 mark that requires the model to generate an answer, from instruction following to mathematics, reasoning and code, yet barely changes MMLU, which we score by option likelihood. The adapted models also stop answering at length. Their responses shrink toward the short domain answers they were trained on, and the more method shortens responses, the more accuracy it loses (3). The adapted models thus stop behaving as the assistants they were, even though likelihood-based probes change little. Replaying an earlier models predictions is standard remedy for such losses (Li and Hoiem, 2016; Buzzega et al., 2020). distillation penalty, however, constrains the model only at the prefixes where it is applied, so the choice of replay inputs decides which behavior is protected. Recent selfgenerated replay for instruction-tuned models samples from beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, outside the chat template (Marek et al., 2026), and context-free synthetic data likewise avoids external prompts (Bansal and Sanghavi, 2025). Selfsynthesized rehearsal does use instruction contexts, but it synthesizes and refines them and trains on the refined outputs (Huang et al., 2024). What has not been isolated is which ingredients of replay matter: where the reference model is matched, whose responses are replayed, and in what form. To study this question, we introduce InstructReplay, minimal form of instruction-context replay (Figure 1). The initial model answers 9,600 general instructions once, and during domain training the model matches the frozen initial models full next-token distributions on these saved responses. We compare it with seven domain-adaptation methods and with three controlled variants. The first keeps the objective but applies it elsewhere, to samples generated from beginning-of-sequence token or to the domain answers themselves. The second matches sampled tokens instead of full distributions, and the third replays the instruction Figure 1: Overview of InstructReplay. (a) Before training, the frozen initial model M0 answers each general instruction once under its chat template, and these assistant turns form the replay buffer; the datasets own answers are not used. (b) In each step the student matches M0s full next-token distribution at every saved prefix of the replayed turns while it learns domain answers with cross-entropy; the two losses share the students weights. (c) Equalweight mean acquisition and forgetting over six modeldomain settings, combining the adaptation methods in Table 3 and replay controls in Table 4. The green star marks InstructReplay; shading indicates = > 0. datasets own answers instead of the models. Our findings are: Factual fine-tuning mainly damages generative behavior. Standard fine-tuning lowers the four generative benchmarks by 35 points on average and at least halves response length, while likelihood-scored MMLU barely moves (3). Instruction-context replay removes most forgetting while keeping acquisition on par with standard fine-tuning. Replaying the models own answers to general instructions reduces the average general decline from 28.1 to 2.4 points, and its acquisition stays within two points of standard fine-tuning in every setting (6.1). What is replayed matters more than how it is matched. Moving the same constraint from the domain answers to unprompted samples and then to the models own instruction responses reduces the average IFEval decline from 43 to 14 and then to about 3 points. Under sampled targets, replaying the datasets answers to the same instructions instead of the models own more than doubles forgetting, from 3.1 to 7.5 points, whereas soft and sampled targets perform similarly (6.2).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Learning new facts by fine-tuning. Facts that model does not already know are learned more slowly than known ones and, once learned, increase hallucination (Gekhman et al., 2024), and retrieval augmentation outperforms unsupervised fine-tuning for knowledge injection (Ovadia et al., 2024). We take closed-book fine-tuning as given and study its cost to general behavior. Preserving earlier behavior. Parameter-space penalties such as EWC protect weights deemed important for earlier tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017); low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2022) learns less and forgets less than full fine-tuning (Biderman Function-space methods instead et al., 2024). match an earlier models outputs: Learning without Forgetting distills the old model on new-task inputs (Li and Hoiem, 2016), Dark Experience Replay stores logits alongside rehearsed examples (Buzzega et al., 2020), and label annealing distills the initial model on the fine-tuning data itself (Yang et al., 2024b). Rehearsing small share of earlier tasks preserves abilities in sequentially finetuned language models (Scialom et al., 2022). Responses become short, and shortening predicts the loss. Median responses to IFEval prompts shrink from 190 to 20 words, and MATH500 solutions from 242 to 42; Table 2 shows an example in which request for letter receives single sentence. This matches the training data: domain answers average about 30 tokens, while the initial models answers to general instructions average about 340. Spearmans ρ is 0.77 on IFEval, 0.81 on MATH-500 and 0.84 on BIG-Bench Hard (Appendix J). The losses are not only word-count failures. 3 Naive SFTs IFEval pass rate falls by 11 points on length constraints but by 55 points or more on constraints that require structure or specific content, such as formats, required openings and endings, and combined constraints (Appendix Table 25). Among questions that M0 answers correctly, the failure rate of adapted models is lowest, below 20%, when response stays within 25% of M0s length, and far higher when it is much shorter or much longer (Figure 2b). What predicts failure is thus departure from M0s response, of which shortening is the most common form. Hypothesis. Fitting short domain answers shifts the models behavior in assistant turns toward terse, direct answers, which breaks instruction following and chain-of-thought formatting; knowledge probed by likelihood is affected far less. If the hypothesis holds, retention penalty should be most effective when it is applied in the contexts where assistant behavior is exercised.

Near θ0, the replay loss is quadratic penalty whose curvature is built only from the logit Jacobians at the replayed prefixes (Appendix A). It resists parameter changes that alter the models outputs in those contexts and leaves other directions unconstrained. sections.title: 7 Analysis
sections.content: Replay source. The diagnosis in 3 ties the loss of general ability to responses that drift away from M0s. Replay counters this drift best when its targets are M0s own responses in assistant turns. Domain-answer prefixes cover only short factual answers, and BOS samples lie outside the chat template. The datasets answers are assistant turns in different style, so fitting them moves the model away from M0 in another direction (Appendix H). Gold replay keeps M0s MATH-500 response length yet loses 4.3 points there, against 0.2 for InstructReplay, so matching length alone does not preserve accuracy. Updates driven by models own outputs have likewise been found to forget less than training on external targets (Shenfeld et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Knowledge-level changes. InstructReplay keeps assistant behavior close to M0s, and its MMLU score changes little, by 1.35 points on average. The largest change, 4.56 on CommonCorpus SmolLM3, does not come from output format, since the four options keep nearly all of the probability mass at the scored position, as they do for M0. It also varies across training runs (Appendix G). Retention weight. We chose λ = 0.25 among {0, 0.25, 1, 4} on CommonCorpus with SmolLM3 and Qwen3, where it gave the highest for both (Appendix E). Relative to no replay, which at λ = 0 is identical to Naive SFT, the selected replay 8 weight lowers from 25.10 to 4.66 for SmolLM3 and from 20.33 to 1.40 for Qwen3. Larger weights trade acquisition for retention unevenly: at λ = 4, Qwen3 forgets slightly less but loses quarter of its acquisition. Because λ was selected on these two settings, the four transfer settings, Phi-4-mini and all of PMC, are the fairer test of the recipe, and there InstructReplay leads the strongest baseline by 5.16 points or more in S. Cost. InstructReplay doubles the sequences per step and replays about 3M response tokens per model, roughly an order of magnitude more than its domain tokens. Yet its PMC training takes at most 2.22 GPU-hours per model, against at least 4.83 for RAFT, and the buffer is generated once per model and shared across domains (Appendix E).

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Fine-tuning small instruction-tuned models on new facts mainly damaged their generative behavior: generative benchmarks collapsed and responses shrank, while likelihood-scored MMLU barely moved. Replaying the initial model on general instructions largely prevented this damage at little cost to acquisition. In the controlled comparisons, assistant-turn replay gave lower average forgetting than BOS-conditioned and domain-answer replay, and self-generated answers gave lower average forgetting than the tested dataset answers. Soft and sampled targets performed similarly at the shared coeﬀicient. For practitioners, about ten thousand general instructions answered once by the model being adapted are an inexpensive safeguard. Small MMLU declines under replay and larger models remain open.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Evaluation. Domain acquisition relies on model judges without human calibration, judges of the same families also score RAFTs training targets, and invalid-vote rates differ between methods. Some evaluation questions cue part of the answer. Publication dates alone cannot rule out that related facts appeared in pretraining. Coverage of general ability. Our evaluation covers five general benchmarks that overlap in kind with the replay mixture; whether retention extends to abilities absent from the replay data, such as safety behavior or long-context use, remains untested. MMLU is scored by likelihood and is therefore insensitive to generation failures. Comparisons. The replay controls use the shared settings in 5.3; configuration differences and the Gold replay formatting diagnostic are detailed in Appendix H. Method-specific tuning remains open. The study covers three models from different families, all at the 4B scale, two domains and short training (300 steps), and the six settings share general-benchmark questions and are therefore not independent.

sections.title: Ethics and Reproducibility
sections.content: Biomedical scores measure factual answering about research articles and do not support clinical use. PMC sources were selected for CC BY 4.0 licenses; the UltraData repository declares Apache2.0 and requires compliance with incorporated upstream licenses, and full-text redistribution awaits row-level clearance. The accompanying supplement provides the paper source, result tables, hashanonymized domain labels, scoring materials and verification script (Appendix I).

sections.content: The arXiv ancillary files provide result tables for all 114 evaluated endpoints, hash-anonymized domain labels and the scoring materials. The standalone supplement also includes the LaTeX source. The result tables give the five General scores, the domain confirmation count and A, and of every endpoint, together with the paired intervals, output lengths and training costs. The labels cover 102 endpoints: the 54 rows of Table 3, the 36 additional training runs and the 12 BOS replay and Hard runs. For each endpoint they give the three judge votes and the majority label on all 512 questions, and the CommonCorpus eligibility mask is included. The scoring materials contain the dataconstruction and judge prompts, the data cards, the source examples of Appendix B, saved short General outputs and the BBH answer extractor. verification script recomputes every labeled endpoints confirmation count from the judge votes, the A, and values from the scores, the confirmation transitions and the unknown-only ranges of Appendix B.4. It uses the Python standard library only. Released examples include two attributed CC BY 4.0 source excerpts with example questionanswer pairs, short General outputs and six complete BBH response examples. Full source and evaluation corpora are withheld because rowlevel redistribution permission is not established for the complete data mixture. All models are public. Student repositories are: HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B Qwen/Qwen3-4B microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct Judge and fusion repositories are: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B google/gemma-4-31B-it openai/gpt-oss-20b The recorded training runtime uses Transformers 4.57.1; judge deployment logs report vLLM 0.19.0. For each checkpoint and generative benchmark we take the median response length and divide it by that of the same models M0. Table 24 averages these ratios over the six settings, and Figure 7 relates them to the accuracy change of every adapted checkpoint. The Spearman correlation over the 60 adapted checkpoints is 0.77 for IFEval, 0.81 for MATH-500 and 0.84 for BBH. The 60 exclude the six Gold replay checkpoints; Table 24 adds their length ratios, and including them gives correlations of 0.80, 0.73 and 0.74. Gold replay keeps M0s MATH-500 length (ratio 1.00) yet loses 4.3 points there, which agrees with the question-level result below: departure from M0s response, not shortening alone, goes with failure.
